# How to Hire and Pay Remote Contractors as a Non-US Resident Running a US LLC in 2026

Running a US LLC from abroad gives you incredible leverage. But the moment you start hiring contractors, the compliance layer gets real fast. Here is exactly how to do it right.

---

## Why Contractor Compliance Matters More Than You Think

The IRS does not care where you live. If your US LLC pays contractors, you have reporting obligations. Getting this wrong means penalties, audit flags, and payment delays that kill momentum.

The good news: the system is straightforward once you understand the two variables that drive every decision.

**Variable 1: Where is the contractor located?**
**Variable 2: Where is the work performed?**

These two answers determine your paperwork, your withholding obligations, and which tools you should use to pay.

---

## The Two Contractor Categories You Will Deal With

### US-Based Contractors

If you hire someone with a US address and a Social Security Number (SSN) or Employer Identification Number (EIN), the standard rules apply.

- Collect a **W-9 form** before the first payment
- Issue a **1099-NEC** if you pay them **$2,000 or more** in a calendar year (this threshold increased from $600 beginning in 2026 and will be indexed for inflation going forward)
- File 1099s with the IRS by January 31 each year
- Penalties for missing 1099s start at $60 per form and climb to $340 per form for late filing; intentional disregard carries a minimum penalty of $680 per form with no maximum cap

> **Note:** If your contractor is a registered C-Corp or S-Corp, you generally do not need to issue a 1099-NEC. Confirm their entity type on the W-9.

### Non-US Contractors (Foreign Nationals Working Outside the US)

This is where most LLC owners relax too much. If a foreign contractor performs work entirely outside the United States, that income is considered foreign-sourced and is not subject to US tax withholding.

You still need to:

- Collect a **W-8BEN** (for individuals) or **W-8BEN-E** (for entities) before paying
- Keep the signed form on file for at least 3 years
- Do NOT issue a 1099-NEC for foreign contractors

> **Note:** If a foreign contractor performs any work on US soil, the rules change entirely. When in doubt, consult a US tax professional.

---

## Contracts: What Every Contractor Agreement Needs

A solid contract protects your LLC and reinforces the contractor classification. Without it, the IRS or a court could reclassify your contractor as an employee, triggering back payroll taxes and penalties.

Every contractor agreement for your US LLC should include:

- **Independent contractor classification clause:** Explicit statement that the worker is not an employee
- **Scope of work:** Specific deliverables, not job titles or ongoing duties
- **Payment terms:** Rate, currency, payment schedule, and method
- **IP assignment:** All work created is owned by the LLC upon payment
- **Termination clause:** Either party can end the agreement with reasonable notice
- **Governing law:** Specify which US state governs the contract (use your LLC's state of formation)

Tools like [Bonsai](https://www.hellobonsai.com) and [Dubsado](https://www.dubsado.com) offer contractor agreement templates you can customise and send digitally.

---

## Best Tools to Pay International and US Contractors in 2026

| Tool | Best For | Key Feature |
|---|---|---|
| **Deel** | Foreign contractors | Built-in W-8BEN collection, local compliance |
| **Wise Business** | International transfers | Low FX fees, multi-currency accounts |
| **Gusto** | US contractors and mixed teams | Automated 1099-NEC filing |
| **Remote.com** | Global contractor management | Contract templates by country |
| **PayPal / Payoneer** | Simple one-off payments | Wide global access |

For most non-US LLC owners managing a small remote team, **Deel** handles the heaviest compliance lifting. It collects the right tax forms, stores them, and flags when forms expire.

---

## Your Annual Contractor Compliance Checklist

Use this every January to stay clean with the IRS.

- [ ] W-9 or W-8BEN on file for every contractor paid in the prior year
- [ ] Tally total payments per contractor across all invoices
- [ ] Issue 1099-NEC to every US contractor paid $2,000 or more by January 31
- [ ] File 1099 information returns with the IRS (via Gusto, Track1099, or Tax1099)
- [ ] Archive all contractor agreements and payment records for a minimum of 4 years

> **Note:** If you use Gusto or Deel for payments, most of this is automated. The manual work only applies if you are paying contractors directly through bank transfers or PayPal.

---

## Common Mistakes That Trigger IRS Problems

- Paying a US contractor without collecting a W-9 first
- Forgetting to file 1099s because "they are just a freelancer"
- Using the same contractor for years at set hours without a contract, which looks like employment
- Letting W-8BEN forms expire (they are valid for 3 years, then must be renewed)

---

## Ready to Build a Compliant Remote Team?

Getting the structure right from day one saves you thousands in penalties and hours of back-and-forth with the IRS.
